name: Clownfish
habitat: Sheltered reef flats and lagoons, living inside host anemones
description: Bright orange with white bands, clownfish live their whole lives partnered with a single sea anemone. A special mucus coating protects them from the anemone's stinging cells. They are territorial and will boldly inspect snorkellers passing near their home.
funFact: All clownfish are born male — the dominant fish in a group can change sex to become female.

name: Blue Tang
diet: Algae it grazes off coral and rocks
habitat: Coral reefs, often in loose schools
description: Juveniles are vivid yellow; adults shift to royal blue with a yellow tail spine. Blue tangs graze algae that would otherwise smother coral, making them vital reef gardeners.
funFact: The 'surgeonfish' name comes from a scalpel-sharp spine at the base of the tail — handle a tangled one with care.

name: Queen Angelfish
habitat: Deep reef slopes and ledges, often in pairs
description: One of the Caribbean's most striking fish: electric blue and yellow with a dark crown-like spot. Usually seen in pairs patrolling the reef, they are curious and will approach snorkellers slowly.
funFact: They are known to hybridise with the closely related blue angelfish.

name: Stoplight Parrotfish
habitat: Coral reefs from shallow flats to fore-reefs
description: Parrotfish crunch coral with beak-like teeth to reach algae, then excrete the grit as sand. Males shimmer turquoise and pink; females and juveniles are mottled red-brown.
funFact: A single large parrotfish can produce hundreds of kilograms of beach sand each year.

name: Sergeant Major
habitat: Shallow reefs, jetties and rocky areas in huge schools
description: Named for its five black stripes, this hardy damselfish forms pulsing schools over shallow reefs. During breeding, males turn bluish and fiercely guard egg patches on rock faces.
funFact: The males guard their purple egg patches so diligently they will even chase much larger fish away.

name: Great Barracuda
habitat: Reefs, seagrass beds and open water near shore
description: A sleek, silver torpedo with an underslung jaw of jagged teeth. Barracuda are curious and may shadow snorkellers, but attacks on people are extremely rare. Avoid wearing flashy jewellery that can look like prey.
funFact: Barracuda have no swim bladder, so they must keep swimming — you'll rarely see one hover.

name: Nassau Grouper
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky ledges
description: A thick-bodied, curious reef predator with distinctive 'tattoo' bars across its head. Nassau groupers famously approach divers and can change colour to communicate mood.
funFact: Once a year, thousands gather at the same spawning sites on the full moon — sadly, this predictability has made them easy to overfish.

name: Moorish Idol
habitat: Clear reef flats and slopes
description: Elegant black, white and yellow bands with a long dorsal filament. They drift in pairs or small groups along the reef crest, picking at sponges in crevices.
funFact: Despite the name, they are unrelated to the 'Gill' character fish they inspired in Finding Nemo.

name: Blue Regal Tang
habitat: Outer reef slopes, schooling above coral heads
description: The vivid cobalt-blue surgeonfish with a black palette marking and yellow tail. They form loose feeding schools that hover above the reef, drifting with the current.
funFact: Juveniles are bright yellow with blue fins before growing into adult colours.

name: Titan Triggerfish
habitat: Sandy reef flats and coral gardens
description: Large, leathery and territorial. When guarding their nest chamber, titan triggerfish will aggressively charge intruders — including snorkellers — and can deliver a serious bite.
funFact: Nesting females bite and ram anything above the nest, so swim backwards and away along the seabed — the territory is an upward cone.

name: Blacktip Reef Shark
habitat: Shallow lagoons and reef flats
description: A slender, shy shark with unmistakable black fin tips, commonly seen patrolling shallow lagoons in small groups. They avoid people and are easily startled by splashing.
funFact: Some can speed-burst at nearly 20 km/h when chasing prey over the reef flat.

name: Whitetip Reef Shark
habitat: Caves and overhangs, resting by day
description: Recognisable by white-tipped dorsal and tail fins, these sharks rest in caves during the day and hunt alone at night. Snorkellers often see them lying quietly under ledges.
funFact: They can pump water over their gills, letting them rest motionless on the seabed — most sharks must swim to breathe.

name: Reef Manta Ray
habitat: Cleaning stations and plankton-rich coastal waters
description: Graceful giants that glide on 5 m wings, barrel-rolling to feed on plankton. Each manta's belly spots are unique, like a fingerprint. Completely safe to swim alongside.
funFact: Mantas have the largest brain-to-body ratio of any fish and appear to recognise individual divers.

name: Green Sea Turtle
habitat: Seagrass meadows, lagoons and reef flats
description: The classic reef turtle: paddling serenely over seagrass beds or resting under coral ledges. Keep distance, never touch or chase, and give them room to surface and breathe.
funFact: Green turtles can hold their breath for hours while resting — but a startled swimmer can stress them into fleeing.

name: Hawksbill Turtle
habitat: Coral reefs, especially crevices and drop-offs
description: Smaller than the green turtle with a hawk-like beak and amber shell plates. Hawksbills are the reef's sponge-eaters, keeping fast-growing sponges from overgrowing coral.
funFact: Their beautiful 'tortoiseshell' pattern made them a target for the souvenir trade, which devastated populations.

name: Bottlenose Dolphin
habitat: Coastal bays, estuaries and open water
description: Playful, social and intelligent, bottlenose dolphins sometimes approach swimmers and surfers to surf bow waves. Enjoy from a distance — they are wild animals with their own schedules.
funFact: Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.

name: Lionfish
habitat: Reef crevices, overhangs and wrecks
description: Striped red-and-white lionfish with feather-like pectoral fins and venomous dorsal spines. In the Caribbean and Atlantic they are an invasive plague that devours young reef fish.
funFact: A sting is extremely painful but rarely deadly — heat (45°C water) on the wound breaks down the venom.

name: Reef Stonefish
habitat: Coral rubble, sandy flats and weedy areas
description: The most venomous fish known: a lumpy, camouflaged ambush predator that looks exactly like a rock. Dorsal spines inject a severe venom — shuffle your feet and never grab 'rocks'.
funFact: Stonefish can survive 24 hours out of water — a stranded one is still dangerous.

name: Giant Moray Eel
habitat: Caves and holes in the reef
description: A thick green eel with a menacing mouth permanently agape — it's just breathing. Morays are shy and retreat into holes, but feeding or provoking them can cause serious bites.
funFact: Morays have a second set of jaws in their throat that lunges forward to drag prey in.

name: Common Octopus
habitat: Rocky reefs, lairs marked by shell middens
description: A master of camouflage that shifts colour and skin texture in a heartbeat. Octopuses are curious and intelligent; if one studies you from its den, hold still and let it look.
funFact: An octopus has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood.

name: Broadclub Cuttlefish
habitat: Coral reefs and sandy slopes
description: The chameleon of the sea: cuttlefish ripple waves of colour across their skin to hypnotise prey and talk to each other. They hover like small hovercraft, steering with skirt-like fins.
funFact: Cuttlefish are colourblind — yet they match background colours perfectly using polarised light cues.

name: Box Jellyfish
size: Bell to 30 cm, tentacles to 3 m
habitat: Warm coastal waters, especially after rain and on calm evenings
description: Transparent and nearly invisible in the water, box jellyfish are among the most venomous animals in the sea. In northern Australia stinger season runs roughly October to May — swim inside stinger nets or wear a full stinger suit.
funFact: Unlike most jellyfish, box jellyfish have eyes — 24 of them, some with lenses and retinas.

name: Moon Jellyfish
habitat: Calm coastal waters, drifting in groups
description: A translucent saucer with four horseshoe gonads visible on top. Its sting is mild for most people — a slight tingle on sensitive skin. Swarms can fill quiet bays after onshore winds.
funFact: Moon jellies have been studied by NASA — thousands flew aboard space shuttle Columbia in 1991.

name: Starry Pufferfish
habitat: Reef slopes and lagoons
description: A slow, charming reef resident that inflates into a spiky balloon when threatened. Their flesh and organs contain tetrodotoxin, a deadly poison — never touch or eat them.
funFact: Tetrodotoxin is up to 1,000 times more toxic than cyanide, with no known antidote.

name: Raccoon Butterflyfish
habitat: Reef slopes and lagoons, often in pairs
description: Butterflyfish are the reef's ballet dancers — flat, vividly patterned fish that flit between coral branches in pairs. Their 'eyeband' patterns confuse predators about which end is the head.
funFact: Butterflyfish are so faithful to their partners that marine biologists use them as a gauge of reef health.

name: Bluestreak Cleaner Wrasse
diet: Parasites and dead skin picked off clients
habitat: Fixed 'cleaning stations' on the reef
description: These tiny wrasse set up service points where big fish — even sharks — queue up to have parasites nibbled off. They perform a hypnotic zigzag dance to advertise.
funFact: Some sneaky blenny fish mimic cleaners, then take a bite of fin instead — the reef's own con artists.

name: Humphead Wrasse
diet: Molluscs, fish, starfish and even toxic crown-of-thorns
habitat: Steep outer reef slopes
description: The giant of the wrasse family, with a distinct hump above the eyes and pouty lips. These gentle, inquisitive giants may follow snorkellers around the reef like oversized puppies.
funFact: They are one of the few predators that eat crown-of-thorns starfish, protecting corals from outbreaks.

name: Garibaldi
habitat: Kelp forests and rocky reefs
description: California's state marine fish: a blazing orange damselfish that darts through kelp gardens. Males cultivate neat red-algae lawns to impress females and guard the nest fiercely.
funFact: The male chirps at intruders by grinding throat teeth together — a sound divers can hear underwater.

name: Leafy Sea Dragon
habitat: Kelp and seagrass in southern Australia
description: A seahorse relative draped in leaf-like appendages that sway with the kelp, making it nearly invisible. Look closely — spotting one is a badge of honour for snorkellers.
funFact: The male carries the bright pink eggs on a brood patch under his tail until they hatch.

name: Blue Groper
habitat: Rocky reefs and kelp beds
description: Big, friendly and famously inquisitive — blue gropers follow snorkellers around New South Wales reefs like tour guides. Despite the name, females are brownish and juveniles green.
funFact: They crunch sea urchins with plate-like teeth, keeping kelp forests grazed clean.

name: Dusky Grouper
habitat: Rocky reefs and wrecks
description: The Mediterranean's gentle giant, often found resting beside boulders and approaching divers with calm curiosity. Long-lived and slow to reproduce, it has declined from overfishing.
funFact: Dusky groupers start life female and turn male as they grow — like many groupers.

name: Mediterranean Parrotfish
habitat: Rocky and Posidonia seabeds
description: Females are a rosy red-orange; males a slate blue-grey with a bright tail edge. Like their tropical cousins, they graze algae and help keep Mediterranean rocky reefs balanced.
funFact: Until genetics settled it, scientists argued for decades whether the colourful sexes were separate species.

name: Ballan Wrasse
habitat: Kelp and rocky reefs
description: A stocky, thick-lipped wrasse in mossy greens and blues that crushes shellfish with strong throat teeth. Often tame around snorkellers in the northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean.
funFact: Ballan wrasse change colour with age and sex — and can live more than 30 years.
